findings.title: Missing `prisma` import causes runtime ReferenceError
findings.body: The new code added in this PR calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: ... } })` (line 96) but `prisma` is not imported in this file. The imports end at `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. Hitting the salesforce CalendarService code path (which happens on every salesforce CalendarService instantiation that goes through `getClient`) will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined`, breaking salesforce bookings entirely for everyone — including self-hosters that never opt into credential sharing. This is an immediate runtime crash for a previously-working integration.

findings.title: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is invalid zod; every sharing-mode response is rejected
findings.body: The schema uses computed object keys `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. `z.string().toString()` returns the schema's typeName (e.g. `"ZodString"`), so the produced keys are the literal strings `"ZodString"` and `"ZodOptional"`, not catch-all matchers. The schema therefore requires the response object to contain numeric properties literally called `"ZodString"` and `"ZodOptional"`, which no real OAuth response ever has. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` then unconditionally throws `"Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"` whenever `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is true. Consequence: every refresh-token call routed through credential sharing fails; the outer `try/catch` blocks in the integrations then return the stale, expiring auth and token refresh silently regresses. This is the central defect that breaks the new sync path.

findings.title: Refresh token is overwritten with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: After a successful parse, the function unconditionally does `if (!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token) { refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"; }`. Whenever the parsed payload lacks `refresh_token` (which is true for every credential-sharing response, since the broken schema above never retains one), the real refresh token is replaced in-memory with the placeholder literal `"refresh_token"`. The integrations then write this garbage value into the database (`prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`). Future refresh attempts will send the literal string `"refresh_token"` to the OAuth provider and fail with `invalid_grant`, permanently invalidating the credential. Even outside sharing mode, any integration whose schema makes `refresh_token` optional will silently corrupt its stored refresh token.

findings.title: Sharing-mode return type incompatible with most callers
findings.body:
When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId` is true, the function returns whatever `fetch(...)` yields — a `Response` object — and never reads its body. The signature is typed as `() => any`, and each integration expects a specific post-shape immediately after the call:

- `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94-96` does `const token = res?.data; ... token.access_token; token.expiry_date` — `Response` has no `.data`, so this throws and the surrounding try/catch returns the stale auth.
- `packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192` does `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn * 1000` — `Response` has no `.expiresIn`, producing `NaN`, and the prisma update writes `NaN` into `expiryDate`.
- `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96` does `tokenInfo.data.error` — `Response.data` is `undefined`, so `.error` throws.
- `packages/app-store/zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:217` does `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` — same issue.
- `packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:84` passes the `Response` straight into `handleLarkError`, which then attempts `data.data.refresh_expires_in`. Without a documented sync-endpoint shape, Lark silently breaks the moment the response format is not exactly what the local refresh returned.

The other integrations (office365calendar, office365video, webex, zoomvideo) happen to call `handleErrorsJson`/`handleWebexResponse`/`handleZoomResponse` which accept a `Response`, but they then rely on `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (which is itself broken — see other findings), so they are still non-functional in sharing mode. Result: the feature advertises support for many apps but, in practice, breaks every app that opts in.

findings.title: findFirst-then-create is not atomic; webhook can produce duplicate credentials
findings.body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst(...)` followed by `prisma.credential.create(...)` if no row matches, with no transaction and no unique constraint to lean on. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appId)` will both observe no row and both insert a new credential, leaving the user with multiple rows for the same app — a state the rest of the codebase assumes does not happen (e.g. lark's callback, webex/zoom/office365 callbacks all explicitly delete pre-existing rows). The `findFirst` lookup also doesn't filter by `type`, so when the same `appId` exists with multiple legacy `type` values, an update may be applied to the wrong row. The docstring even acknowledges this with "Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id of the credential", but a race-free approach (e.g. `prisma.credential.deleteMany({ userId, appId })` inside a transaction, or an upsert on a composite key) would be safer.

findings.title: Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method and has no body-size, replay, or method check
findings.body: The handler does not check `req.method`, so any method with the correct secret header (e.g. GET, PUT) reaches the database mutation path; only the secret comparison and `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` flag gate it. There is also no body-size limit, no timestamp/nonce, and no signature scheme beyond a static shared secret. Combined with the fact that anyone in possession of `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` can create or replace credentials for any userId in the system, an attacker who learns or leaks the secret (e.g. via logs, env backups) can rewrite every user's app tokens by replaying the request. At minimum, restrict to POST and verify a recent timestamp.

findings.title: Uncaught zod and decryption errors produce 500 with stack trace
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws on malformed body and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...))` throws on a tampered or wrong-key payload. There is no error boundary, so callers receive a default 500 plus Next.js's full error page with stack trace, leaking file paths and internals. The function should catch `ZodError`/`Error` and respond with a structured 4xx (e.g. 400 for invalid body, 422 for decryption failure) — and crucially never echo the offending key bytes.

findings.title: Credential sync endpoint contract is undefined and inconsistent across integrations
findings.body: The function POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` (form-urlencoded) to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and returns the raw response unmodified. But each integration expects the response to have a different exact shape: google expects `{access_token, expiry_date}`, office365 expects `{access_token, expires_in, refresh_token?}`, hubspot expects a full `HubspotToken`, lark expects `{data:{access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`, etc. Self-hosters implementing the parent endpoint have no documentation describing these required shapes (or the URL/return value must instead be customized per app — which contradicts the function being shared). Without a clear spec, the feature is unusable in practice.

findings.title: Outbound call to sync endpoint has no authentication from Cal.com side
findings.body: `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` is sent with no headers, no signature, and no client identity. The receiving service has no way to verify that the call came from this Cal.com instance or that `appSlug`/`calcomUserId` weren't tampered with by a network attacker or a mis-routed proxy. Combined with the fact that `userId` is trusted blindly to look up tokens server-side, anyone who can intercept traffic to the configured endpoint can impersonate any user. The endpoint should require a Cal.com-issued signature (e.g. an HMAC of the body using a shared key) so the parent service can reject forged refresh requests.

findings.title: No tests cover the new credential-sharing sync path
findings.body: The PR introduces three pieces of behavior with no test coverage: the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` webhook (including auth/secret checking, decryption, and the find/update/create branches), `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts` (sharing vs. non-sharing branches, including what the returned value looks like to callers), and `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts` (the broken minimum-token schema and the refresh-token overwrite). The PR description explicitly states no tests were added and existing tests were not run. Given the multiple integration-affecting bugs above, merging without tests risks regressing every OAuth integration.
